projects.title: Data-Centric Land Cover Classification
projects.subtitle: Label Noise Ranking via Fine-Tuned SAM & SAM2 Geospatial Auto-Segmentation
projects.description: A seven-step Kaggle competition pipeline that ranks satellite training patches by their level of label noise — not by building the best model, but by identifying which labels are most trustworthy. Uses a fine-tuned Segment Anything Model (SAM) and a SAM2 geospatial auto-segmentation model to score and rank each training patch.
projects.detailed_description: This project tackles the Kaggle Data-Centric Land Cover Classification Challenge, where the objective is to rank training samples by label noise rather than maximise model accuracy. The pipeline consists of seven ordered notebooks: (1) Data Visualization to explore patches and define a PyTorch SegmentationDataset; (2) Fine-tuning facebook/sam-vit-base with DiceCE loss for 10 epochs, producing per-image IoU scores; (3) Threshold Scoring to batch-run inference and export IoU CSVs; (4) Ranking Model Setup to convert (image, mask) pairs into 4-channel tensors for a DataLoader; (5) SAM2geo Auto-Segmentation using segment-geospatial to generate agreement-ratio scores; (6) SAM2 Threshold Scoring to refine per-image scores; and (7) Combined Score Ranking that merges both score streams, trains a small UNet regressor, and outputs the final submission. The combined score formula (IoU × (1 + 0.1 × auto_score)) rewards samples that both models agree are clean, placing cleaner labels earlier in the ranking.
features: Seven-notebook end-to-end pipeline from raw patches to final submission CSV
Fine-tuned facebook/sam-vit-base (mask decoder only) with DiceCELoss over 10 epochs
Per-image IoU scoring pipeline with batch inference and CSV export
SAM2 geospatial auto-segmentation for independent agreement-ratio scoring
4-channel tensor DataLoader for UNet ranking regressor training
Combined noise score: IoU × (1 + 0.1 × auto_score)
Dual-model consensus — images both models agree are clean ranked highest
Reproducible: pinned requirements.txt and sequential notebook execution order
GPU-accelerated (CUDA) for all inference and training loops
outcomes: Produced submission_33.csv — final ranked image list for Kaggle evaluation
Demonstrated a data-centric approach to label-noise detection in satellite imagery
Achieved dual-model score fusion (SAM + SAM2) for more robust noise estimation
Built a reusable PyTorch SegmentationDataset for land cover patch datasets
Established a template pipeline for label-noise ranking in geospatial ML challenges

pipeline_steps.description: Load & visualise training patches and noisy label masks; define SegmentationDataset
Fine-tune facebook/sam-vit-base (mask decoder only) using DiceCE loss for 10 epochs
Batch inference with saved checkpoint; export IoU scores CSV
Build 4-channel tensors from (image, mask) pairs and wrap in DataLoader
SAM2 geospatial auto-segmentation for independent agreement-ratio scores
Threshold and refine SAM2 predictions to produce clean per-image scores
Merge SAM + SAM2 scores, train UNet regressor, output final submission

projects.title: Urban Utility Network Explorer
projects.subtitle: Satellite + Street-Level Intelligence for Bengaluru's Power Grid
projects.description: An end-to-end Python GIS pipeline that downloads real OSM utility infrastructure data for Bengaluru, enriches it with satellite imagery from Google Earth Engine, and serves interactive analysis through a Streamlit dashboard — network tracing, flood risk, vegetation encroachment, and terrain analysis all in one command.
projects.detailed_description: Urban utility networks are increasingly vulnerable to climate-driven risks. This project builds a reproducible, production-ready GIS pipeline integrating OpenStreetMap infrastructure data with four Google Earth Engine satellite datasets (DynamicWorld LULC, SRTM terrain, Sentinel-2 NDVI, and JRC Global Surface Water). The core analysis identifies which substations lie in flood-prone zones, which power lines face vegetation encroachment risk, and which grid segments cross steep terrain. A Streamlit dashboard with Folium interactive maps, network graph tracing (Dijkstra), and outage simulation visualizes the full risk picture. The pipeline runs end-to-end with a single command and includes a synthetic offline demo mode requiring no GEE authentication.
features: Live OSM data download — real power lines, substations & towers for Bengaluru
500 m service-area buffer analysis and spatial joins
Network graph model with Dijkstra shortest-path tracing
GEE flood risk mapping (JRC GSW) — 50.6% of substations in flood-prone zones
Sentinel-2 NDVI vegetation risk — 188 km of lines at encroachment risk
SRTM terrain slope analysis — 321 km of lines crossing steep terrain (>15°)
5-tab interactive Streamlit dashboard with toggleable satellite + OSM layers
Offline synthetic demo mode — no GEE account needed
Fully reproducible: pinned dependencies, deterministic seed (seed=42), EPSG:4326 / UTM 43N
outcomes: Identified 89 of 176 substations (50.6%) in flood-prone zones
Flagged 188 km of power lines at vegetation encroachment risk
Detected 321 km of grid lines crossing steep terrain (>15° slope)
Integrated 4 GEE satellite datasets with real-time OSM network data

projects.title: GEE Utilities
projects.subtitle: Curated Google Earth Engine Scripts & Notebooks for Geospatial Analysis
projects.description: A curated collection of lightweight, self-contained Google Earth Engine utility scripts and Jupyter notebooks covering essential geospatial workflows — from Land Surface Temperature estimation and LULC classification to spatial sampling, raster-to-vector conversion, and temporal image filtering.
projects.detailed_description: GEE_Tools is a practical, open-source toolkit built to streamline recurring geospatial operations in Earth observation research. Each utility is independently usable, requiring no inter-script dependencies. The collection spans both the GEE JavaScript Code Editor and the Python API via Jupyter notebooks. Workflows include: randomized spatial sampling with configurable buffer zones, Landsat 8 Land Surface Temperature retrieval using split-window and single-channel algorithms, date-driven satellite image selection and compositing, raster-to-vector format conversion using GeoPandas and Rasterio, study area boundary definition and Folium-based visualization, and supervised LULC classification using GEE's built-in ML classifiers (Random Forest, SVM, CART). The toolkit is designed for reproducibility — all scripts are self-documented and ready to run after GEE authentication and a single pip install.
features: Random Points Buffer (01): Randomized spatial sampling with configurable buffer radii for field survey design
LS8 LST Estimation (02): Land Surface Temperature retrieval from Landsat 8 thermal bands using GEE JavaScript
Date-Wise Image Selection (03): Temporal satellite image filtering and compositing by custom date ranges
Raster to Vector (04): Automated conversion of raster outputs to vector formats (Shapefile/GeoJSON) using GeoPandas
Study Area Map (05): Interactive boundary definition and choropleth visualization with Folium
LULC GEE ML (06): Supervised Land Use/Land Cover classification using GEE's Random Forest, SVM, and CART classifiers
Each utility is self-contained — no inter-script dependencies
Supports both GEE JavaScript Code Editor and Python API workflows
MIT licensed and open for community contributions
outcomes: 6 production-ready geospatial utilities covering the full RS processing pipeline
Reduces repetitive boilerplate in Earth observation research workflows
Supports studies in thermal analysis, land cover change detection, and spatial sampling
Jupyter notebooks are reproducible with a single pip install + GEE authentication
Dual-environment support: GEE Code Editor (JS) and Python API (Jupyter)

projects.title: Maximum Snow Cover Area — NW Himalaya
projects.subtitle: Monthly Maximum Snow Cover Extent Analysis of the Northwest Himalayan Region (2000–2020)
projects.description: A 20-year (2000–2020) analysis of monthly maximum Snow Cover Area (SCA) over the Northwest Himalaya using MODIS/Terra MOD10A2 V6 satellite data. Implements a multi-tile mosaicking, reprojection, and pixel-wise monthly maximum snow detection pipeline — underpinning a peer-reviewed Remote Sensing journal publication.
projects.detailed_description: The Northwest Himalaya (NWH) is one of the world's most climatically sensitive regions, acting as the primary freshwater reservoir for millions of people through snow and glacier melt. This study built an end-to-end satellite data processing pipeline using the MODIS/Terra Level-3 8-day composite Snow Cover product (MOD10A2 V6, 500 m resolution) spanning March 2000 to February 2020. The spatial domain covers four MOD10A2 tiles (h23v05, h24v05, h24v06, h25v06) representing the full Northwest Himalayan extent. The pipeline performs: (1) date-sorted file organisation from NASA Earthdata, (2) four-tile mosaic generation per 8-day period, (3) reprojection to EPSG:4326, (4) rectangular clipping to study area bounding box, (5) precise boundary clipping via shapefile, and (6) monthly maximum SCA computation — where any pixel recording DN=200 (snow) in at least one 8-day observation within a month is classified as snow. This conservative maximum approach reduces cloud contamination bias. Results were published in a peer-reviewed article in Remote Sensing (MDPI, Q1 journal) exploring the response of NWH snow cover dynamics to climate variability.
features: 20-year MODIS snow cover time series: March 2000 – February 2020
Four-tile mosaic pipeline covering the full Northwest Himalayan extent (h23v05, h24v05, h24v06, h25v06)
500 m spatial resolution using MOD10A2 V6 Level-3 8-day composite product
DN-class-aware pixel filtering: snow (DN=200), cloud (DN=50), lake ice (DN=100), no-snow (DN=25)
Monthly maximum SCA: pixel marked snow if any 8-day observation within the month shows DN=200
Automated date-based file sorting from NASA Earthdata filenames
Shapefile-based precise boundary clipping (bounding box + exact polygon)
Reprojection pipeline: native sinusoidal → EPSG:4326
Backed by a peer-reviewed Remote Sensing (MDPI) journal publication
outcomes: Published in Remote Sensing 2021, 13(4), 655 (MDPI — Q1 journal)
Quantified 20-year snow cover dynamics across the Northwest Himalaya
Demonstrated the climate sensitivity of NWH snow cover to temperature and precipitation variability
Provided a reproducible Python pipeline for MODIS SCA analysis
Contributed to regional water resource and hydropower planning research

projects.title: BharatBench
projects.subtitle: A Benchmark Dataset for Data-Driven Weather Forecasting over India
projects.description: A ready-to-use dataset and benchmarking framework designed to accelerate data-driven weather forecasting research over India. Derived from IMDAA reanalysis with pre-processed, ML-ready data optimized for limited computational resources.
projects.detailed_description: BharatBench addresses the gap in regional weather forecasting research by providing a high-quality dataset specifically tailored to the Indian monsoon region. Unlike global datasets like WeatherBench (ERA5), BharatBench focuses on the meteorologically distinct Indian subcontinent with complex orography (Himalayas, Western Ghats) and diverse microclimates. The dataset spans 31 years (1990–2020) with 6-hourly temporal resolution, covering surface variables (2m temperature, wind, pressure, precipitation) and 13 pressure levels. With a 32×32 grid at 1.08° resolution, it is trainable on standard laptop CPUs. Complete benchmarks are provided: persistence, climatology, weekly climatology, linear regression, CNN, and ConvLSTM baselines with evaluation code.
features: 31-year IMDAA-derived reanalysis dataset (1990–2020)
Regional focus: 5°N–40°N, 65°E–100°E with 1.08° spatial resolution
6-hourly temporal resolution with 13 pressure levels (50–1000 hPa)
Surface variables: 2m temperature, 10m wind components, sea-level pressure, precipitation
Pressure-level variables: geopotential height, temperature, humidity, wind components
Pre-processed and ML-ready — 32×32 grid points for low compute barrier
Trainable on standard laptop CPU (Intel i7 / 32 GB RAM sufficient)
Complete baseline implementations: persistence, climatology, linear regression, CNN, ConvLSTM
Standard evaluation metrics: RMSE, MAE, Anomaly Correlation Coefficient (ACC)
Kaggle dataset and Jupyter notebook tutorials included
outcomes: Published research paper on arXiv
Publicly available Kaggle dataset
Comprehensive benchmark results for 3-day and 5-day lead times
4 Jupyter notebooks with complete reproducible code
Baseline CNN model achieves 26.27 RMSE vs. 28.47 climatology baseline
ConvLSTM baseline achieves 26.87 RMSE, capturing temporal dynamics

projects.title: Personal Portfolio Website
projects.subtitle: Multi-Page Academic Portfolio with Flask & Static Site Generation
projects.description: A professional, statically-generated academic portfolio built with Flask and Frozen-Flask. Features multi-page layouts, data-driven content from JSON, responsive design, and dual deployment to GitHub Pages and Netlify via GitHub Actions.
projects.detailed_description: A full-stack portfolio website that demonstrates modern web development practices. Built with Flask for dynamic route generation and Frozen-Flask for static site compilation, the portfolio serves content from JSON data files ensuring separation of concerns. The site features a responsive design with custom CSS, JavaScript interactivity, and optimized asset delivery. Deployment is fully automated — every push to the main branch triggers GitHub Actions to rebuild the static site and deploy to both GitHub Pages and Netlify. Includes security headers (X-Frame-Options, X-XSS-Protection, X-Content-Type-Options) and asset caching strategies.
features: Multi-page layout: home, about, projects, publications, contact, CV views
Data-driven architecture: all content sourced from JSON (profile, projects, CV data)
Responsive design with custom CSS and JavaScript
Interactive project filtering and detailed project pages

Dual deployment: GitHub Pages (via Actions) + Netlify (automatic)
Security headers: X-Frame-Options, X-XSS-Protection, X-Content-Type-Options
Asset caching: 1-year immutable cache for static resources
Search engine optimization (SEO) ready

Fully automated CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions
100% static site — no server overhead, instant load times

projects.title: Academic CV Builder
projects.subtitle: Python-Based PDF CV Generator for Researchers
projects.description: A Python tool that generates publication-ready academic CVs from a single JSON data file. Features a clean, professional layout with embedded profile images, clickable social icons, and DOI/URL hyperlinks — all without requiring LaTeX or manual PDF formatting.
projects.detailed_description: CV_Builder streamlines the process of creating and maintaining academic CVs. Instead of manually formatting a resume in Word or LaTeX, researchers simply edit a single JSON file containing their profile, experience, education, publications, and skills. The tool uses ReportLab to programmatically generate a polished PDF with precise layout control. Key features include profile image embedding with automatic square-cropping, clickable social profile icons (email, phone, LinkedIn, GitHub, Google Scholar, ResearchGate) in the header, and embedded hyperlinks for publication DOIs and URLs. Work experience entries are automatically sorted chronologically with current roles pinned at the top. The modular architecture makes it easy to add, remove, or reorder CV sections.

Clickable social icons in the header (email, phone, LinkedIn, GitHub, Scholar, ResearchGate)

Pre-defined CV styles for consistency: CVName, CVTitle, CVContact, CVSectionHeading, CVBody, CVPublication, CVJobTitle, CVOrganization, CVBullet
Support for multiple entry types: journals, conference papers, posters, training, webinars
Auto-generated footer with 'Last updated' timestamp
Fully customizable — maintain separate JSON files for different application contexts (academic vs. industry CVs)
